Everything downstream depends right, worth checking rather assuming: Getting wrong single common way produce confidently incorrect answer. index function collides silently encodes different problem, solver answers one correctly, nothing anywhere reports error.
code: n_vertices <- 10 n_colours <- 3  # variable for "vertex v has colour c" vc <- function(v, c) (v - 1L) * n_colours + c ids <- as.vector(outer(seq_len(n_vertices), seq_len(n_colours), vc)) c(distinct = length(unique(ids)), expected = n_vertices * n_colours,   max = max(ids)) #> distinct expected      max  #>       30       30       30

title: Modelling a problem as SAT
text: proper colouring two conditions. vertex gets exactly one colour, edge joins two vertices colour. first cardinality constraint, sat_exactly() encodes . second plain clause per edge per colour: endpoints can take colour c. variable count print exactly 10 * 3 = 30, worth noticing: sat_exactly() added variables . three literals per constraint, forbidding every pair three clauses, "auto" used pairwise encoding. Push numbers switches counter introduce auxiliaries — next section comes .
code: colouring_solver <- function(n_colours, edges, n_vertices) {   vc <- function(v, c) (v - 1L) * n_colours + c   s <- sat_solver()    # exactly one colour per vertex   for (v in seq_len(n_vertices)) {     sat_exactly(s, vapply(seq_len(n_colours), function(c) vc(v, c), numeric(1)), 1)   }    # adjacent vertices differ   for (i in seq_len(nrow(edges))) {     u <- edges[i, 1]     w <- edges[i, 2]     for (c in seq_len(n_colours)) {       sat_add(s, c(-vc(u, c), -vc(w, c)))     }   }    s }  s <- colouring_solver(3, edges, 10) s #> <zusat_solver> cadical-3.0.1 #>   variables:      30 #>   active clauses: 85

code: s2 <- colouring_solver(3, edges, 10) ours <- seq_len(10 * 3)  projected <- sat_solutions(s2, vars = ours, limit = 200) sat_n_solutions(projected) #> [1] 120 sat_complete(projected) #> [1] TRUE pairwise <- sat_solver() sat_at_most(pairwise, 1:6, 2, encoding = "pairwise")  sequential <- sat_solver() sat_at_most(sequential, 1:6, 2, encoding = "sequential")  c(pairwise = sat_n_vars(pairwise), sequential = sat_n_vars(sequential)) #>   pairwise sequential  #>          6         16 c(   everything = sat_n_solutions(sat_solutions(sequential, limit = 500)),   projected = sat_n_solutions(sat_solutions(     sat_solver() |> (\(s) {sat_at_most(s, 1:6, 2, encoding = "sequential"); s})(),     vars = 1:6, limit = 500   )) ) #> everything  projected  #>         80         22

Ask two solver says : "unsat" strong claim — “find one” “none exists” — default taking solver’s word . proof turns something independent tool can check, trusting neither zusat CaDiCaL: proof checkable, file checker reads must contain every clause proof relies . rules adding exactly-one constraints sat_exactly() : clauses go solver, list hold. Written hand need auxiliary variables — two colours, exactly-one one “least one” clause one “” clause per vertex — list can go : Now solver file see exactly formula: Hand two files DRAT checker: whole point section. claim “two-colouring exists” now checkable program never heard zusat CaDiCaL. trade visible code : sat_exactly() convenient picks better encoding numbers grow, clauses live inside solver. need self-contained CNF hand another tool, build list . satisfiable answer needs proof, model evidence — check , exactly .
code: s3 <- colouring_solver(2, edges, 10) sat_status(sat_solve(s3)) #> [1] "unsat" colouring_clauses <- function(n_colours, edges, n_vertices) {   vc <- function(v, c) (v - 1L) * n_colours + c   clauses <- list()    for (v in seq_len(n_vertices)) {     lits <- vapply(seq_len(n_colours), function(c) vc(v, c), numeric(1))     clauses <- c(clauses, list(lits))                        # at least one     for (pair in utils::combn(n_colours, 2, simplify = FALSE)) {       clauses <- c(clauses, list(c(-lits[pair[1]], -lits[pair[2]])))  # not both     }   }    for (i in seq_len(nrow(edges))) {                          # adjacent differ     for (c in seq_len(n_colours)) {       clauses <- c(clauses, list(c(-vc(edges[i, 1], c), -vc(edges[i, 2], c))))     }   }   clauses }  two_colours <- colouring_clauses(2, edges, 10) length(two_colours) #> [1] 50 proof <- tempfile(fileext = ".drat") cnf <- tempfile(fileext = ".cnf")  s4 <- sat_solver()            # empty: tracing records the whole derivation sat_trace_proof(s4, proof)    # so it must start before any clause  sat_add(s4, two_colours) sat_status(sat_solve(s4)) #> [1] "unsat" sat_close_proof(s4)           # the proof is incomplete until this returns  write_dimacs(two_colours, cnf) c(clauses = length(readLines(cnf)) - 1L, proof_steps = length(readLines(proof))) #>     clauses proof_steps  #>          50          21 drat-trim problem.cnf problem.drat #> c 15 of 50 clauses in core #> s VERIFIED

title: zusat 0.1.0
text: First release. Solves Boolean satisfiability problems bundled copy CaDiCaL solver, external solver required. sat_solve() solves formula incremental solver, returning type-stable data frame variable assignments. sat_solutions() enumerates models, vars project onto variables matter. read_dimacs() write_dimacs() format every solver benchmark set speaks. sat_limit() bounds hard solve may work, solve can return "unknown" rather running indefinitely. sat_constrain() adds clause one solve ; sat_fixed() reports literals proved root; sat_simplify() runs inprocessing alone. sat_at_most(), sat_at_least() sat_exactly() encode cardinality constraints, choosing pairwise sequential-counter encoding automatically. sat_trace_proof() sat_close_proof() record DRAT LRAT proof unsatisfiability, checkable external tools drat-trim.
